# Faculty of Arts — Building Plan (Footprint, Zoning and Finalized Materials)

**Stage:** university-plan (post-survey, all six faculty surveys read)
**Site:** flat, level ground, ~60 m × 60 m (≈3,600 m²); stratified (layered) soil,
generally suitable for standard shallow spread-footing foundations.
**Brief:** lecture halls/classrooms for a mid-sized faculty, staff offices, and a
cafeteria/canteen serving students and staff.

This plan finalizes the footprint/zoning and the material choices for the Arts
building, in particular the cafeteria. It is built on my own survey
(`SURVEY_ARTS.md`) and on the five peer surveys, which I have now read in full.
Section 5 states explicitly what a peer's survey changed and what it did not.

---

## 1. Site strategy (finalized)

The site facts are unchanged from my survey: flat, level, layered soil. The two
governing risks remain **water** (a level site cannot shed water by fall) and
**differential settlement** (bearing capacity is not uniformity on a layered
profile). Both are carried into this plan as design requirements, not deferred
details.

**Foundations (final).** Shallow reinforced-concrete pad footings under columns
and strip footings under load-bearing walls, founded on the verified bearing
stratum, tied together by a **reinforced ground-beam / tie-beam grid**. A
**borehole / trial-pit grid across the whole footprint** — not one central hole —
is a precondition of the foundation design, and must include the cafeteria
corner. Column bases are kept on a single stratum where possible; where a
stratum transition crosses the footprint, footings are stepped or deepened
across it. A **stiffened strip or raft** is held in reserve for the spine and any
bay that cannot avoid a transition. Ground-floor slabs and drainage are detailed
to tolerate small differential movement (movement joints, flexible service
connections, reinforcement detailed for it). No piling is anticipated.

**Drainage and levels (final).** The building is raised on a **plinth with
finished floor level 450–600 mm above surrounding external ground** (raised from
the 150 mm minimum in my survey — see §5), with a graded perimeter apron and a
fall away from the building on all sides. Stormwater is collected by a perimeter
land-drain / French drain plus a positive piped system to the site outfall;
because the site is flat, the **outfall invert and capacity govern the drainage
design** and must be confirmed before the footprint is frozen. Attenuation
(below-ground crate storage or a shallow basin) is assumed to be required. All
external circulation is step-free (max 1:20 ramps where levels change).

**Groundwater (final).** In addition to groundwater level and seasonal
variation, the ground investigation must explicitly check for a **perched water
table** sitting on a lower-permeability stratum — a specific layered-soil risk
(see §5). Sulphate/aggressive ground chemistry and any made ground or buried
obstructions are also to be established before the concrete mix and buried
services are fixed.

---

## 2. Footprint and zoning (final)

**Concept: a three-zone "L" on a central spine, with the cafeteria as a distinct,
fire-separated, structurally independent block at ground level.**

- **Zone A — Teaching (north/west, the larger area).** Two large flat-floor
  lecture halls (approx. 200 and 120 seats) plus a cluster of general teaching
  rooms. The quietest, most acoustically sensitive functions, placed away from
  the site entrance and from the kitchen service yard. The large spans here drive
  the structural grid.
- **Zone B — Staff offices (east edge).** Cellular and small-group offices along
  a naturally lit edge, with a separate, quieter entrance and direct access to
  the teaching zone. Lower floor-to-floor than the teaching zone; the step in
  height breaks the massing and houses plant.
- **Zone C — Cafeteria/canteen (south, at the main student route).** Dining hall
  plus kitchen, servery and stores, at ground level, positioned for public and
  student access **without crossing the teaching zone**, with its own external
  entrance so it can operate outside faculty hours and serve the wider campus.
  It has its own service yard, delivery access and bin store on the site
  boundary. The kitchen is a separate fire compartment (§4).
- **Spine.** A single circulation spine links A, B and C, doubling as the
  accessible route and the primary escape route. It is the one element crossing
  the whole site, so it is kept on a simple regular grid and its foundations are
  the first place the stratified-soil caution is applied.

**Indicative areas (feasibility order-of-magnitude, to be tested):**

| Element | Indicative area |
|---|---|
| Lecture halls / classrooms | ~1,100 m² |
| Staff offices + support | ~600 m² |
| Cafeteria: dining + servery | ~450 m² |
| Kitchen, stores, back-of-house | ~250 m² |
| Circulation, WCs, plant, storage | ~500 m² |
| **Total gross** | **~2,900 m²** |

At ~2,900 m² gross on a 3,600 m² plot, the building is a **two-storey** solution
with a footprint of roughly 1,500–1,700 m², leaving the balance for the entrance
square, service yard, cycle parking and landscaping. A single-storey scheme would
consume nearly the whole plot and leave no external amenity. The cafeteria is
kept at ground level for deliveries, drainage falls and student access; teaching
sits above and beside it.

**Grid.** A regular structural grid (indicatively 7.5 m × 7.5 m for teaching and
office bays, widened locally for the large lecture halls) keeps foundations
repetitive — exactly what the layered-soil condition rewards — and lets the
cafeteria's different servicing needs be a local variation rather than a
site-wide complication.

**Phasing (final).** The teaching block and offices are built first; the
cafeteria block is structurally and services-independent and can follow as a
second phase without disrupting teaching (see §5).

---

## 3. Primary construction materials — building generally (final)

**Structure: reinforced concrete frame with steel long-span roof over the
lecture halls.**

- *Reinforced concrete* for columns, cores and general floor plates: robust and
  low-maintenance; good acoustic mass between stacked teaching floors; inherent
  fire resistance without added protection; and a stiff, monolithic frame that
  tolerates and redistributes small differential movements better than a light,
  articulated one.
- *Structural steel* for the long-span roofs over the large lecture halls, where
  a column-free span is functionally necessary. Steel is fire-protected
  (intumescent coating or board) and the roof build-up is detailed for acoustic
  separation from the floor below.
- *Foundations:* shallow reinforced-concrete pad/strip footings per §1, with a
  raft held in reserve for the spine and any bay crossing a stratum transition.

**Envelope: brick/block masonry cavity wall with a ventilated rainscreen or
render, and aluminium-framed double-glazed windows.** Masonry is durable,
low-maintenance, thermally massive and acoustically good, is familiar and
repairable for a public institution, and gives the fire separation between zones
for free. Insulated cavity with a drained and ventilated outer leaf; thermally
broken aluminium windows with double glazing and solar control to the south/west
teaching elevations. Roof: warm flat roof (insulated, single-ply membrane) over
the general building, with a pitched or standing-seam metal roof over the large
halls if span and drainage favour it.

**Internal finishes (general teaching/office):** painted plasterboard or plaster
on masonry, suspended acoustic ceilings in teaching rooms, carpet or vinyl in
offices, hard-wearing vinyl or sealed screed in circulation. These are the *dry*
finishes and are deliberately **not** carried into the kitchen.

**Services:** natural ventilation with openable windows and stack effect for
teaching and offices, with mechanical ventilation only where required (kitchen,
WCs, internal rooms). Heating via a low-temperature water system with radiators
or underfloor in the dining hall.

---

## 4. Cafeteria/canteen — finalized materials and construction

The cafeteria is the most demanding part of the brief: a long-span public dining
space combined with a commercial kitchen that is simultaneously a **fire
hazard**, a **wet/hygiene zone**, and a **high-maintenance** area. The four
criteria named in the brief — structural span, fire rating, hygiene/moisture
resistance, maintenance — are addressed in turn.

**Structural span (dining hall).** Column-free or near-column-free to allow
flexible seating and servery layouts: indicatively a **12–15 m clear span**,
achieved with a steel roof structure (beams or a shallow truss) on concrete
columns, or a post-tensioned concrete slab if the floor above requires it. The
kitchen, by contrast, is a cellular, heavily serviced space on a tight grid. The
two are structurally different and are deliberately separated by a
movement/fire joint so the long-span dining volume and the stiff kitchen box do
not fight each other.

**Fire rating.** The kitchen is a high fire-hazard compartment, separated from
dining, teaching and office areas by a **60-minute fire-rated wall with
self-closing fire doors** (confirm against the local code and fire strategy).
The dining hall is a separate compartment from the teaching zone. Escape routes
from the dining hall are direct to outside, not through the kitchen.

**Hygiene and moisture resistance.** Kitchen and dishwash zones get
non-combustible, non-porous, washable surfaces throughout:

- Walls: stainless-steel or FRP panels, or cement/glass-mat board — **not**
  paper-faced gypsum board, which grease vapour and sustained moisture destroy
  and which cannot be washed.
- Ceilings: a washable, non-porous, non-combustible system — **not** a standard
  suspended mineral-fibre ceiling, which is unsuitable in a commercial kitchen.
- Floors: coved, slip-resistant, tanked wet-area finish with falls to drains and
  a grease trap/interceptor on the drainage line. The kitchen floor build-up is
  deliberately different from the dry teaching floors.
- Dining hall: hard-wearing, easily cleaned floor (sealed screed or heavy-duty
  vinyl/tile), washable wall finishes to splash height, and a ceiling that can be
  cleaned.

**Kitchen exhaust and suppression.** Grease-laden cooking vapour is a recognised
fire hazard: grease accumulates on duct walls, can ignite from a cookline
flare-up, and fire can travel inside the duct through otherwise fire-separated
compartments. Therefore:

- A dedicated, continuously welded or flanged **liquid-tight grease duct** (not
  ordinary galvanised spiral duct), with access doors at every change of
  direction for cleaning.
- The duct enclosed in a fire-rated shaft, or given a listed fire-rated wrap,
  where it passes through or adjacent to other occupancies; terminated well clear
  of air intakes, windows and combustible roof build-up.
- A dedicated **kitchen suppression system** (hood + duct), interlocked to shut
  down the supply fan and fuel on activation.
- A grease trap/interceptor on the drainage line.

**Maintenance.** All kitchen surfaces are chosen to be cleanable and repairable
by the institution's own maintenance team: stainless and FRP panels are
replaceable in sections; the grease duct has cleaning access by design; the
dining floor is a single, repairable finish. The kitchen is on the ground floor
with direct service-yard access so deliveries, waste and duct cleaning do not
pass through teaching or office space.

**Zoning consequence.** These are not finishes-level details — they drive the
ceiling void depth (grease duct and its fire enclosure), the roof penetrations
and shaft locations, the drainage falls and the compartmentation of the
cafeteria block. They are therefore fixed here, in the zoning layout, not
deferred.

---

## 5. Influence of peer surveys — what changed and what did not

I read all five peer surveys in full. Two of them changed a decision I would
otherwise have made; the rest confirmed decisions already taken or were
inapplicable to a flat site. I state each explicitly.

### 5.1 Changes I made because of a peer's survey

**(a) Plinth / finished floor level — changed. [Faculty of Law; also Faculty of
Medicine]**
My survey set finished floor level at a **minimum of 150 mm** above surrounding
external ground. The Law survey specifies a raised plinth of **450–600 mm**, and
the Medicine survey independently specifies **~450–600 mm**, both on the same
reasoning: on a level site with no natural fall, the plinth is the cheapest and
most reliable defence against ponding and against water tracking back into the
building. I have **raised my FFL to 450–600 mm** (§1). This is a genuine change
to a decision in my own survey, driven by two peers reaching the same conclusion
on the same site condition. It has a knock-on effect on the entrance thresholds
and the accessible-route design, which are now set out to suit the higher plinth.

**(b) Perched water table — added. [Faculty of Medicine; also Faculty of Law]**
My survey listed "groundwater level and seasonal variation" as a condition to
verify but did not name the specific layered-soil risk. The Medicine survey
identifies a **perched water table** held on top of a less permeable stratum as
the condition that matters more than the regional water table on layered ground,
and the Law survey lists the same risk. I have **added an explicit perched-water
check** to the ground investigation (§1). It affects foundation depth, the
drainage design, and confirms my decision to rule out any basement or
semi-basement.

**(c) Cafeteria as an independent phase and a campus-facing facility — firmed
up. [Faculty of Law]**
The Law survey makes two points I had not stated: the cafeteria should be
**structurally and services-independent so it can be built as a second phase**
without disrupting teaching, and it should be able to **operate outside faculty
hours and serve the wider campus**. My survey already placed the cafeteria for
public/student access without crossing the teaching zone; I have now made the
**phasing** explicit in §2 and firmed up the **own-external-entrance /
out-of-hours operation** requirement in Zone C. This is a change of emphasis
that affects the zoning and the fire-separation strategy (the cafeteria block
must stand alone as a compartment and as a services entity).

### 5.2 Peer findings that confirmed decisions already taken (no change)

- **[Faculty of Computing] Grease-laden kitchen exhaust as a fire hazard.**
  Already adopted in my survey and carried into §4 unchanged: dedicated
  liquid-tight grease duct, cleaning access doors at every change of direction,
  fire-rated shaft/wrap, termination clear of intakes/windows/combustible roof
  build-up, hood+duct suppression interlocked to fan and fuel, grease trap, and
  60-minute kitchen separation. The Computing survey is the origin of this
  finding; my survey had already adopted it, so nothing further changed.
- **[Faculty of Business] Kitchen/dishwash finishes and compartmentation.**
  Already adopted in my survey and carried into §4 unchanged: no paper-faced
  gypsum or mineral-fibre ceilings in kitchen/dishwash zones; non-combustible,
  non-porous, washable wall and ceiling surfaces; 60-minute kitchen compartment;
  coved, slip-resistant, tanked wet-area floors with falls to drains, distinct
  from the dry teaching floor build-up.
- **[Faculty of Engineering] Wet-zone material schedule.** The Engineering
  survey's kitchen specification (cementitious board, masonry or tiled concrete;
  resin/epoxy or safety-vinyl screed with coved skirting and trapped channel
  drainage; washable metal/vinyl-faced ceilings; 60–120 min non-combustible
  enclosure, easier in masonry/concrete than lightweight drywall) is consistent
  with my §4 and required no change. It does reinforce the point that the
  kitchen's fire separation is easier to achieve in masonry/concrete than in
  lightweight drywall, which is consistent with my masonry-envelope and
  concrete-frame decisions.
- **[Faculty of Medicine] Cafeteria material schedule and "no basement".** The
  Medicine survey's cafeteria table (RC frame with long-span beams/ribbed slab;
  1–2 hour kitchen compartmentation; ceramic tiling, stainless splashbacks,
  coved floors with grease trap; vapour-control layer and ventilated roof
  build-up over the kitchen; stainless benches and replaceable modular ceiling
  panels) agrees with my §4 and required no change. Its decision to rule out a
  basement on a flat, layered site with a possible perched water table matches my
  own reasoning.

### 5.3 Peer content that does not apply to my site (stated, not fabricated)

- **[Faculty of Engineering] Hillside-specific strategy.** The Engineering site
  is a hillside with an ~18 m cross-fall; its terracing, retaining walls, slope
  stability analysis, cut-off drains and stepped footings are responses to that
  slope and have **no application to my flat, level plot**. I have not imported
  them. The one Engineering point that does transfer is the general principle of
  a **short, direct kitchen extract route to a roof termination**, which my §4
  already satisfies by placing the kitchen against the service yard with a
  dedicated vertical shaft and roof penetration.
- **[Faculty of Engineering] "Adopted the Arts stratified-soil caution."** This
  is my own finding being used by a peer, not a peer finding affecting me; it
  changes nothing in my plan.

### 5.4 Net effect

Two peer surveys changed decisions in my plan: **Law and Medicine** raised my
plinth/FFL from a 150 mm minimum to 450–600 mm, and **Medicine and Law** added an
explicit perched-water-table check. **Law** also firmed up the cafeteria's
independent phasing and out-of-hours, campus-facing operation. The Computing,
Business, Engineering and Medicine cafeteria findings confirmed the material and
fire decisions I had already made and required no change. The Engineering
hillside strategy was assessed and found inapplicable to my flat site. No peer
finding was rejected without reason, and I have not claimed a connection that is
not really there.

---

## 6. Feasibility risks and next steps

- **Differential settlement on layered soil** — the principal geotechnical risk;
  resolved by the footprint-wide borehole grid and the foundation strategy in §1.
  A single central borehole must not stand in for a footprint-wide investigation.
- **Perched water table** — to be confirmed by the ground investigation; affects
  foundation depth and drainage design.
- **Flat-site drainage** — outfall invert and attenuation capacity to be
  confirmed before the layout is fixed; the raised plinth (450–600 mm) is the
  first line of defence.
- **Kitchen fire strategy** — compartmentation, duct enclosure and suppression to
  be developed with the fire engineer; they constrain the zoning, not just the
  finishes.
- **Two-storey assumption** — to be tested against the accommodation schedule; if
  the brief grows, the plot is the binding constraint, not the structure.
- **Next steps:** footprint-wide ground investigation (including a perched-water
  check); drainage/outfall survey; fire strategy workshop; accommodation schedule
  to confirm areas and storey count; confirmation of the cafeteria's independent
  phasing and out-of-hours access strategy.

---

*Status: complete. This is a feasibility-level building plan; foundation design,
drainage capacity and fire strategy remain subject to confirmation by boreholes,
a site-wide drainage study, and the fire authority respectively.*
